COSMOS finds no multivitamin or cocoa effect on blood biomarkers

In a randomized COSMOS ancillary study with 498 to 506 participants, neither a daily multivitamin nor cocoa extract changed two-year trajectories of plasma N-terminal tau, neurofilament light or oligomeric amyloid-beta; every treatment-versus-placebo comparison was nonsignificant.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed randomized placebo-controlled biomarker analysis•September 23, 2026

COSMOS finds no multivitamin or cocoa effect on blood biomarkers

In a randomized COSMOS ancillary study with 498 to 506 participants, neither a daily multivitamin nor cocoa extract changed two-year trajectories of plasma N-terminal tau, neurofilament light or oligomeric amyloid-beta; every treatment-versus-placebo comparison was nonsignificant.

Key quantitative results: Multivitamin versus placebo produced no significant difference in yearly change for NT1 (3.7%, 95% CI -3.0% to 10.8%; p=0.29), NfL (3.1%, -1.9% to 8.3%; p=0.23) or oligomeric amyloid-beta (-8.9%, -23.9% to 9.0%; p=0.31).

BiomarkersClinical TrialsBloodNeurofilament lightN-terminal tau fragmentPharmacodynamic research

Added September 24, 2026 · NCT02422745; DOI:10.1177/13872877261489739; PMID:42775737

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The randomized design makes this a cleaner mechanistic test than observational supplement studies. The uniformly null biomarker results weaken claims that the tested multivitamin or cocoa extract affects these blood-marker trajectories over two years, but they do not negate previously reported cognitive findings because NT1, NfL and oligomeric amyloid-beta are not validated surrogate endpoints for prevention benefit.

Study design

COSMOS randomized older US adults in a 2-by-2 factorial design to a daily multivitamin-mineral supplement, cocoa extract containing 500 mg/day of flavanols including 80 mg of epicatechin, both interventions or matching placebos. This ancillary analysis included 506 participants with NT1 or NfL measurements and 498 with oligomeric amyloid-beta measurements and modeled yearly percentage change over two years.

Key quantitative results

  • Multivitamin versus placebo produced no significant difference in yearly change for NT1 (3.7%, 95% CI -3.0% to 10.8%; p=0.29), NfL (3.1%, -1.9% to 8.3%; p=0.23) or oligomeric amyloid-beta (-8.9%, -23.9% to 9.0%; p=0.31).
  • Cocoa extract versus placebo also produced no significant difference for NT1 (-0.7%, 95% CI -7.1% to 6.1%; p=0.83), NfL (0.5%, -4.4% to 5.6%; p=0.85) or oligomeric amyloid-beta (-5.9%, -21.4% to 12.6%; p=0.51).
  • The analysis included 506 participants for NT1/NfL and 498 for oligomeric amyloid-beta; the biomarker outcomes were measured over two years.

What changed

A new randomized analysis now directly tests whether the COSMOS multivitamin and cocoa interventions alter three blood-biomarker trajectories and finds no detectable effect for either intervention.

Strength of evidence

Moderate randomized mechanistic evidence with placebo controls and repeated biomarker measurements. It is an ancillary subset, the confidence intervals permit modest effects, the measures are not validated surrogate endpoints and the abstract does not establish analytical-performance characteristics for the assays.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings do not support using these biomarkers to claim a biological response to the tested supplements or using the supplements to modify these biomarker trajectories. They do not establish absence of cognitive benefit or harm and should not be converted into an Alzheimer treatment recommendation.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to prevention-trial interpretation, pharmacodynamic claims and communication about supplement mechanisms. It separates a null randomized biomarker effect from analytical validity, clinical utility and clinical outcomes.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The report evaluated within-person change in three exploratory neurodegeneration-related blood measures. It did not validate them as surrogate endpoints, establish clinical cutoffs or show that changes predict cognitive benefit.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No assay authorization, availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from the report.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does this prove multivitamins or cocoa have no cognitive effect?
No. It shows no detectable effect on the three measured blood biomarkers over two years; those biomarkers are not validated surrogates for cognitive outcomes.
Are these biomarkers authorized for monitoring supplement response?
No. The paper does not establish an authorized or guideline-endorsed monitoring use.
Why is this both Biomarkers and Clinical Trials?
The primary analysis is a prospective randomized intervention comparison, and its central outcomes are changes in blood biomarkers; both topics independently describe the report's main purpose.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Ancillary subset rather than the full COSMOS randomized population
  • No validated surrogate relationship between these biomarker changes and cognitive benefit
  • Confidence intervals do not exclude modest positive or negative effects
  • Population was older US adults selected for the parent cardiovascular and cancer-prevention trial, not biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer disease
  • No new analytical-validation, cutoff, decision-impact or clinical-utility evidence
